title: The Green Pen Delusion
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles critiques a Research School video showing a teacher running retrieval practice followed by 'tick and fix' corrections in green pen. His argument is that the routine secures compliance, not learning: the colour of the pen is irrelevant to memory, copying out corrections is thoughtless, and accepting blank answers removes the desirable difficulty of attempting retrieval. He observes that teachers voice doubts aloud mid-lesson and then override them to comply, which is one reason teachers stop improving. He then redesigns the sequence so that pupils write one-word answers, the teacher cold calls repeatedly, and corrections are made from memory as a further retrieval. A faster variant uses ten oral questions asked up to three times with no pens at all. The conclusion is that the aim should be to see what pupils still do not know, with minimal teaching effort and maximum retrieval.
points: Routines such as green pen correction produce visible compliance and can be mistaken for evidence of learning.
Pupils must always attempt an answer, because without trying to retrieve they will not notice their misconceptions or attend to corrections.
If most pupils are stuck on a retrieval question, the fault lies in the earlier teaching or curriculum and it should be taught again.
Cold calling many pupils repeatedly gives more retrieval per minute than writing and copying corrections.
Teachers should want to see what pupils still do not know, not tidy corrections.
quotes: But students are then going to “tick and fix”. Will correcting mistakes in green pen make any difference? The answer is no.
These take time, and do nothing to put the information in long term memory. It may help short term memory - but this will be up to the student.

The teacher says, out loud, the thought that is troubling them. This offloads the thought, so they can stop worrying about it. They critique their own teaching live, and then immediately ignore that critique. The opportunity to improve is lost.
Compliance is the goal of the routine, not learning. Her instincts know this. But she has to suppress them.
Then she asks students to chant it back to her. That is performance, it is not recall. It is compliance, but not learning.
Why correct this way? Because it is from memory, another retrieval.
You don’t want to see students’ corrections. You want to see what they still don’t know.
Only one transition. No mini white board. No green pens high in the sky. No corrections at the visualiser. No checking for understanding. No chanting. No interruptions!
context: The author argues pen colour has no effect on how memorable a correction is.
Copying corrections consumes time without securing long-term memory.
Teachers who voice doubts and then ignore them stop improving.
The routine rewards compliance, which differs from learning.
Chanting an answer back is performance and not recall.
Making corrections from memory turns them into more retrieval practice.
Assessment should reveal gaps, not display tidy corrected work.
A pen-free question sequence reduces teacher effort and increases learning.
